passage:
At fifteen, Kunal was made class monitor. By the second week he was writing names on the board for anyone who whispered, telling classmates to fetch his water bottle, and laughing when they grumbled. When Irawati said, 'You never listen when we ask for a change,' he waved her off. 'Rules are rules.' He liked the sound of his own voice carrying across the room.

At twenty-one, Kunal was head of the hostel cultural committee. A first-year, Noor, asked to swap her rehearsal slot because of an exam. 'Not my problem,' he said, scrolling through his phone. That afternoon he moved his own group into the better slot 'just this once'. A senior passing by said, 'You've changed, you know.' Kunal blinked. 'No, I haven't,' he said, and meant it.

qa.q: Who asked to swap a rehearsal slot because of an exam?
How did Kunal's use of authority show the same pattern at fifteen and at twenty-one?
qa.a: Both times he enjoyed being obeyed, waved off a complaint from Irawati or Noor, and bent things his own way, first by bossing classmates and then by taking the better rehearsal slot. At twenty-one he did not notice the change.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he said, 'No, I haven't'?
qa.a: Sure of himself and unaware of the change, so the senior's remark surprised him.

qa.q: What could Kunal do to check his own behaviour?
qa.a: Ask a friend to say honestly how he treats juniors, and listen to complaints like Irawati's before dismissing them.

grounding: The same person's small authority at fifteen and larger authority at twenty-one bring bossiness, less care for others' views and bent rules.
